Based on the healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that not all ethnic groups in New Zealand exhibit socio-economic mortality gradients. While there are socio-economic gradients in health within each ethnic group, they tend to be relatively shallow among Pacific and especially Asian peoples. This suggests that caution should be exercised when applying deprivation or other socio-economic measures as proxy indicators of need for health services.

In contrast, White non-Hispanic New Zealanders tend to have more pronounced socio-economic mortality gradients than other ethnic groups. However, it's essential to note that this does not mean that these groups are inherently "fitter" or more resilient; rather, the socio-economic factors affecting their health may be more pronounced and widespread.

It is also worth noting that the study's findings highlight the need for caution when applying socioeconomic measures as proxy indicators of need for health services across different ethnic groups. A comprehensive understanding of each group's unique social determinants and healthcare needs is necessary to develop effective policies and interventions.
